screens.title: Working with Files for Larger Data
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you’ll learn why and how to work with files on Android when data grows beyond simple key-value pairs. We’ll compare internal storage, which is private to your app and automatically removed on uninstall, with external storage, which is shared and requires care around permissions and security. You will see concrete examples for writing and reading text files using the Context A P I and stream helpers, plus a practical logging activity you can implement in MainActivity. Throughout, we’ll highlight common mistakes—like forgetting to close streams or storing secrets on external storage—so you can avoid them. By the end, you’ll understand getFilesDir and getCacheDir, when to prefer internal storage, and the minimal checks to perform before touching external storage. Think of this as a short toolkit: private sandbox for app files, cached space for temporary data, and guarded public space when you absolutely need it. What file will you store privately first?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Working with Files
Working with Files for Larger Data
Learn when to use file storage, how to read and write text files in internal storage, and essential safety checks for external storage.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Internal Storage

Private to your app, removed on uninstall, ideal for sensitive or app-specific files.

External Storage

Shared and user-visible; good for media but requires permission checks and security thinking.

Read / Write Patterns

Use FileOutputStream/FileInputStream or openFileOutput/openFileInput with Kotlin's use extension to ensure streams close.

Safety Notes

Always handle exceptions, avoid storing secrets on external storage, and check availability before writing to external paths.

Visual concept
Locked safe — internal
Private, app-only, removed on uninstall.
Connecting line metaphor: locked folders inside your app sandbox keep data private.
Explore Key Topics
getFilesDir
Path for persistent internal files; use this for data that should survive app restarts.
openFileOutput
Convenience API that opens a FileOutputStream scoped to internal storage; pair it with the use extension.
External safety
External files are shared and persistent; avoid unencrypted sensitive data and check availability before write.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this set of objectives you’ll focus on the core skills needed to use file storage sensibly on Android. First, you will be able to differentiate internal and external storage by their security, visibility, and lifecycle. Second, you will implement basic code to write and read text files in internal storage using Context helpers and streams, and you will understand how Kotlin’s use extension keeps streams safe. Third, you will recognize the security and lifecycle differences so you can decide where to place data and what will be removed on uninstall. Finally, you will identify the specific Context methods, like getFilesDir and getCacheDir, and know when to use each. Each objective includes a short reason why it matters and a small mnemonic to make the concept memorable. These skills are practical: you’ll apply them in the provided logging activity and in any app that needs to store larger or structured data.

screens.title: Why files instead of SharedPreferences
screens.narratorSegment: SharedPreferences is great for small, simple key-value pairs such as a user setting or a flag, but it’s not the right tool for larger, structured, or binary data. Files provide a more flexible storage model that can hold long text, JSON blobs, images, or logs. For example, a log file that accumulates lines over time or a document that a user edits is better stored as a file than as dozens of preference keys. A common misconception is believing SharedPreferences can replace small databases; while Preferences store simple values, they lack the organization and performance characteristics needed for larger datasets. Files let you choose formats and use streams to read or write large bytes efficiently. In practice, pick files when you need sequential reads or writes, append behavior, or binary content. The key takeaway is matching the storage tool to the shape and size of your data: use SharedPreferences for tiny settings, files for larger documents and binary content, and databases for queryable structured data. Why files instead of SharedPreferences means choose files when data is larger than key-value pairs or when you need appendable or binary storage.. In practical terms, when key-value storage is not enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
Why files instead of SharedPreferences
Match storage choice to data size and shape.
Key properties
  • Files handle large text or binary data and support sequential I/O.
  • Files allow append behavior useful for logs and streaming writes.
  • SharedPreferences is optimized for small, structured key-value pairs, not long blobs.
  • Use files for images, documents, and logs where queryability isn’t required.
Key Takeaway

Files are the right tool for larger or binary content; choose storage by data size and access pattern.

Concrete example
A chat app that stores full conversation history, attachments, or a download cache should use files rather than SharedPreferences. For instance, saving images as files lets you stream bytes and avoid loading everything into memory at once.
Common misconception
Some developers try to store large JSON blobs inside SharedPreferences. This leads to slow reads and harder migration; files or a database are better options.
Pro tip
If you anticipate queries on fields inside the data, prefer a database. Use files when simple read/write or append is sufficient.

screens.title: Internal Storage: getFilesDir and getCacheDir
screens.narratorSegment: Internal storage provides a private sandbox for your app’s files. Two common Context helpers are getFilesDir and getCacheDir. Use getFilesDir for persistent files you expect to keep for as long as the app is installed. Files placed there are private to your app and are removed when the user uninstalls. getCacheDir is for temporary cache files; the system may delete cache files when storage space is low, so never store critical data there. A useful mental model is: filesDir is for content you own and must keep, cacheDir is for content you can recreate. For example, store downloaded thumbnails in cacheDir because you can re-download them; store user documents or logs in filesDir. A common mistake is relying on cacheDir for important data. Another helpful point is permission scope: internal storage requires no runtime storage permissions since it is private. Ask yourself when data must persist beyond restarts and uninstall — if permanence is required, prefer filesDir. Internal Storage: getFilesDir and getCacheDir means choose filesdir for persistent app files and cachedir only for temporary content the system can evict.. In practical terms, private persistent files vs temporary cache. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition Internal Storage
getFilesDir and getCacheDir
Pick persistent app files or temporary cache carefully.
API reminders
getFilesDir(): Returns the path for persistent internal files that survive restarts until app uninstall.
getCacheDir(): Returns the path for temporary cache files; system may delete these when storage is low.
Internal storage does not require external storage permissions because it is private to your app.
Example
Save app_log.txt to getFilesDir so logs remain until uninstall. Save ephemeral thumbnails to getCacheDir since they can be recreated.
Key Takeaway

Use filesDir for persistent app files; cacheDir is for temporary data the system can evict.

Annotation cards
When to pick filesDir
When the user expects the file to remain until uninstall, like logs or user documents.
When to pick cacheDir
When the data can be recreated and you want automatic eviction under low storage.
Misconception check
Don’t assume cacheDir is safe for critical data; it may disappear at any time.

content.html:
Process Flow Write & Read
Write and read a text file in internal storage
A safe code walkthrough using streams and Kotlin's use extension.
Write example (Kotlin)
import android.content.Context
import java.io.File
import java.io.FileOutputStream

fun writeToFileInternal(context: Context, filename: String, content: String) {
    try {
        val file = File(context.filesDir, filename)
        FileOutputStream(file).use {
            it.write(content.toByteArray())
        }
        println("File written to internal storage: ${file.absolutePath}")
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        e.printStackTrace()
        println("Error writing file to internal storage: ${e.message}")
    }
}
Read example (Kotlin)
import android.content.Context
import java.io.File
import java.io.FileInputStream

fun readFromFileInternal(context: Context, filename: String): String? {
    try {
        val file = File(context.filesDir, filename)
        if (!file.exists()) {
            println("File does not exist: ${file.absolutePath}")
            return null
        }
        FileInputStream(file).use {
            val bytes = it.readBytes()
            return String(bytes)
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        e.printStackTrace()
        println("Error reading file from internal storage: ${e.message}")
        return null
    }
}
Explanation
  • Use File(context.filesDir, filename) to target internal storage.
  • Kotlin's use closes streams even when exceptions occur.
  • Check file.exists() to avoid reading missing files.

Process Flow Logging Activity
Logging activity: openFileOutput and openFileInput
Append entries and read full log for debugging.
Starter code excerpt
// inside MainActivity
private val LOG_FILENAME = "app_log.txt"

private fun logEvent(message: String) {
    val timestamp = SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss", Locale.getDefault()).format(Date())
    val logEntry = "$timestamp: $message
"

    try {
        openFileOutput(LOG_FILENAME, Context.MODE_APPEND).use {
            it.write(logEntry.toByteArray())
        }
        Log.d("FileStorageDemo", "Logged: $logEntry")
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        e.printStackTrace()
        Log.e("FileStorageDemo", "Error logging event: ${e.message}")
    }
}
Readback example
private fun readLogFile(): String? {
    try {
        val file = File(filesDir, LOG_FILENAME)
        if (!file.exists()) return null
        openFileInput(LOG_FILENAME).use {
            val bytes = it.readBytes()
            return String(bytes)
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        e.printStackTrace()
        return null
    }
}
Scenario
Call logEvent in onCreate and after key actions, then display the returned string in a TextView or print it to Logcat to inspect the app history.

screens.title: File lifecycle and uninstall behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding file lifecycle helps you set correct expectations for users and designers. Files stored in internal storage are private and deleted when the user uninstalls the app. That makes internal storage a safe place for per-app data you don’t want lingering after uninstall. Cache files in getCacheDir can be removed by the system when the device runs low on storage — they are not guaranteed to persist. External storage has two flavors: app-specific external directories and shared public directories. App-specific external files often get removed on uninstall, while truly public files may persist. A common mistake is assuming external files always survive uninstall; it depends on whether the files are in your app-specific external directory or in public storage. Another pitfall is relying on cache for essential data. The practical rule is to store critical, private data in internal filesDir and use cacheDir only for recreatable artifacts. File lifecycle and uninstall behavior means internal files are removed on uninstall; cache files may be evicted; external persistence depends on where you store the file.. In practical terms, what happens to files when the app is removed or the system needs space. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow Lifecycle
File lifecycle and uninstall behavior
Know where files persist and when they are removed.
Internal files
Private to app. Deleted on uninstall. Use for sensitive or app-specific persistent files.
Cache files
Stored in getCacheDir. The system may delete these when storage is low. Do not store critical data here.
External files
Shared or app-specific external directories. Public files may persist after uninstall; app-specific external files often get removed on uninstall.
Common mistake

Assuming cache is permanent or external is always persistent. Check where you write and the removal semantics for that directory.

screens.title: Internal vs External Storage — Side-by-side
screens.narratorSegment: A clear comparison helps decide where to save different types of files. Internal storage is private to your app, requires no storage permissions, and is removed on uninstall. External storage is shared with other apps and the user, so it requires you to consider permissions and security, and files may persist beyond uninstall depending on the directory. Availability can be an issue for external storage: an SD card may be removed or storage may be mounted to a computer. For sensitive or app-specific files, internal storage is the safer default. If you must use external storage — for example, saving photos the user expects to access outside the app — organize files in app-specific external directories when possible, and avoid saving secrets there. The practical contrast is simple: private and permission-free versus shared and permission-aware. That contrast should guide your default choice: prefer internal storage unless you have a clear sharing requirement. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Warning External Storage
External storage: permissions and availability
Key checks before writing to shared storage.
Permissions

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes developers make when dealing with files; knowing them helps you write robust code. First, forgetting to close streams can leak resources and corrupt data. Use Kotlin's use extension to ensure streams close automatically. Second, not handling IOExceptions and other exceptions leads to crashes when storage is full or files are missing; always wrap file operations in try-catch blocks. Third, storing sensitive data on external storage without encryption exposes users. Fourth, not checking external storage availability can lead to failed writes when the media is unmounted. Finally, confusing cacheDir with filesDir can cause unexpected data loss; cache can be cleared by the system. The practical advice is straightforward: close streams, catch exceptions, prefer internal storage for private data, check storage state before external writes, and encrypt if you must place secrets on shared storage. These habits keep your app stable and your users' data safe. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Create and Read an App Log File
Step-by-step implementation notes and starter snippet.
Steps
  1. Create LOG_FILENAME = "app_log.txt" and TextView with id log_display_text.
  2. Implement logEvent(message) to build timestamp + message and use openFileOutput with Context.MODE_APPEND.
  3. Implement readLogFile() to open the file, read bytes, and return a String or null if missing.
  4. Call logEvent in onCreate and set the TextView text to readLogFile() result.
Starter code (excerpt)
private val LOG_FILENAME = "app_log.txt"

private fun logEvent(message: String) {
    val timestamp = SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss", Locale.getDefault()).format(Date())
    val logEntry = "$timestamp: $message
"
    try {
        openFileOutput(LOG_FILENAME, Context.MODE_APPEND).use {
            it.write(logEntry.toByteArray())
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        e.printStackTrace()
    }
}

private fun readLogFile(): String? {
    try {
        val file = File(filesDir, LOG_FILENAME)
        if (!file.exists()) return null
        openFileInput(LOG_FILENAME).use {
            val bytes = it.readBytes()
            return String(bytes)
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        e.printStackTrace()
        return null
    }
}

In this lesson you’ll learn why and how to work with files on Android when data grows beyond simple key-value pairs. We’ll compare internal storage, which is private to your app and automatically removed on uninstall, with external storage, which is shared and requires care around permissions and security. You will see concrete examples for writing and reading text files using the Context A P I and stream helpers, plus a practical logging activity you can implement in MainActivity. Throughout, we’ll highlight common mistakes—like forgetting to close streams or storing secrets on external storage—so you can avoid them. By the end, you’ll understand getFilesDir and getCacheDir, when to prefer internal storage, and the minimal checks to perform before touching external storage. Think of this as a short toolkit: private sandbox for app files, cached space for temporary data, and guarded public space when you absolutely need it. What file will you store privately first?

In this set of objectives you’ll focus on the core skills needed to use file storage sensibly on Android. First, you will be able to differentiate internal and external storage by their security, visibility, and lifecycle. Second, you will implement basic code to write and read text files in internal storage using Context helpers and streams, and you will understand how Kotlin’s use extension keeps streams safe. Third, you will recognize the security and lifecycle differences so you can decide where to place data and what will be removed on uninstall. Finally, you will identify the specific Context methods, like getFilesDir and getCacheDir, and know when to use each. Each objective includes a short reason why it matters and a small mnemonic to make the concept memorable. These skills are practical: you’ll apply them in the provided logging activity and in any app that needs to store larger or structured data.

This second objectives panel emphasizes practical safety work and the hands-on activity. You will learn to discuss external storage considerations, including when permissions are needed and why external data can be shared beyond your app. You will practice proper error handling for file input and output, catching exceptions such as IOExceptions to avoid crashes. You will learn to spot common mistakes like failing to close streams or writing sensitive data to public storage, and you’ll use the provided logging activity to implement append-style writes and readbacks in an Activity. These objectives prepare you to choose the right storage location, code defensively around file operations, and deliver a simple app log that is both private and recoverable for debugging. Each objective connects to a real behavior: always wrap input and output in try-catch blocks and prefer internal storage for private data.

SharedPreferences is great for small, simple key-value pairs such as a user setting or a flag, but it’s not the right tool for larger, structured, or binary data. Files provide a more flexible storage model that can hold long text, JSON blobs, images, or logs. For example, a log file that accumulates lines over time or a document that a user edits is better stored as a file than as dozens of preference keys. A common misconception is believing SharedPreferences can replace small databases; while Preferences store simple values, they lack the organization and performance characteristics needed for larger datasets. Files let you choose formats and use streams to read or write large bytes efficiently. In practice, pick files when you need sequential reads or writes, append behavior, or binary content. The key takeaway is matching the storage tool to the shape and size of your data: use SharedPreferences for tiny settings, files for larger documents and binary content, and databases for queryable structured data.
